title: Ang 42–53: Guru Arjan
hookLine: the fifth Guru's Sri Rag hymns
tomorrow: what could possibly rank higher than truth?

cards: A car that's sat in a parking lot all afternoon in July. You open the door and the heat comes out at you before you've even sat down. You step back, wait, fan the door, swear a little.
Some days open exactly like that: the inbox, the group chat, the front door, and a wall of heat. The Granth's next voice has a word for that blast. In his Punjabi it's a taata jhola, a hot gust.
So where do you stand when it hits?

teach.h: WHY SO TAKEN WITH WHAT PASSES?
teach.b: From ang 42 to 53 the Sri Rag hymns belong to Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru and Guru Ram Das's son.
His first hymn here opens with a question, in paraphrase: why are you so taken, looking at your children, your partner, your fine clothes? Not because any of them is bad.
Because they pass, and he wants your hands on something that doesn't.
Two pages on, on ang 44, comes his answer, in paraphrase: O my mind, take hold of the shelter of the Lord's Name, and the hot gust won't touch you. Notice the verb.
Take hold, grip, the way you'd grab a railing on a moving bus. Not admire it from across the room.
The Name, Naam, is the Sikh word for the presence of the One, remembered until it's right under your hand when you need it. And notice what he doesn't promise. He doesn't say summer ends.

teach.h: THE HOT GUST WON'T TOUCH YOU.
teach.b: He says the heat won't reach you, the way shade doesn't put out the sun; it changes where you're standing. Tradition says this is also the Guru who gathered these very pages into one book.

teach.h: SAY IT PLAINLY, THEN A PICTURE.
teach.b: You can hear it in him: say it plainly, then give a picture you can carry.
The heat, the shelter, the hand that grips.

how: Sikhs who read the Guru Granth Sahib in order, at home or at the gurdwara, meet Guru Arjan's Sri Rag hymns, headed Mahala 5, right after Guru Ram Das's; some follow along in a Gurbani app or a steek with the meaning beside each line.

s: Guru Arjan tells you to stop loving your family
he asks why we're so taken with what passes; the point is what to hold, not what to drop.
on ang 44, the shelter makes the heat go away
the hymn says the hot gust won't touch you, not that summer ends.
Guru Arjan's Sri Rag hymns follow straight after Guru Ram Das's
ang 40 to 42 is the fourth Guru; from ang 42, the fifth.

games.q: your cousin has three exams, a weekend shift and a phone that won't stop buzzing. she asks for one thing that helps. which fits ang 44?
o: quit the shift. heat is only beaten by getting out of the kitchen.
find one steady thing to grip, a line she can return to between tests.
wait it out. it'll all be over by Friday anyway.
games.why: Guru Arjan's picture is a shelter you take hold of, the Name. the heat comes either way; it just doesn't have to reach you.

practice: Open to ang 44 in a Gurbani app or a steek if one is near, and read one hymn there out loud, slowly, in Gurmukhi or in English, whichever you can.
Then rest in the one picture it gave you: the shelter, your hand on it, the heat outside. Let the rest of the sit be shade.

wordCard.voice: Ang 42. A page of the Guru Granth Sahib, and the page where Guru Arjan's voice enters the first raga.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: ang, a page of the Guru Granth Sahib (the everyday word also means a limb).

carryVoice: For the road: the fifth guru, and a shelter to grip when the hot gust comes. See you tomorrow.
